pages.title: 12 Sets of English Conversation Questions, by Topic
pages.metaTitle: 12 Sets of English Conversation Questions, by Topic (A2-B2)
pages.description: 12 sets of conversation questions for A2-B2 ESL classes: the language each one practises, numbered steps, a variation, and a note for classes of 40 or more.
pages.keywords: ESL conversation questions, English conversation questions by topic, speaking questions for English class, discussion questions ESL, conversation topics for adults learning English
pages.teaches: Conversation practice by topic

hero.text: Twelve sets of conversation questions, graded from A2 to B2, with the language each topic needs and a way to run it that keeps everyone talking rather than one confident learner answering everything.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: Every set gives easier and harder questions, so one page serves a mixed class. The topics are ones any class in any country can discuss safely.

blocks.heading: Making conversation questions actually work
bullets: **Never ask the whole class a conversation question.** One learner answers, thirty listen. Put the questions in pairs or threes, and move round.
**Give the answering language, not just the question.** Two or three phrases on the board - *It depends. I'd say ... The thing is ...* - turn one-word answers into conversations.
**Let them choose.** Pairs pick four questions from the set rather than working through all of them. Choice raises the quality of the answers.
**Thirty seconds of silent thinking first.** With questions of opinion, this is the difference between a real answer and "I don't know".
**Ask for a follow-up, always.** The rule "you must ask one more question after each answer" is what makes it a conversation rather than an interview.
**Change partners once.** The second telling is always better than the first, which is where the fluency gain comes from.

blocks.heading: Everyday life (A2)
text: Concrete topics with simple tenses: safe ground for a class that has not talked much before.

blocks.name: Food and meals
blocks.language: Present simple; *like / prefer*; frequency; food vocabulary
steps: **Easier:** What do you usually have for breakfast? Who cooks in your home? What food do you eat every week? Is there a food you really do not like?
**Harder:** What dish would you cook for a visitor from another country, and why? Has your diet changed in the last five years? Should schools decide what children eat?
Put three phrases on the board first: *It depends. I'd rather ... To be honest, ...*
Pairs choose four questions; after each answer the partner must ask one more question.
blocks.variation: Each learner describes one dish in detail without naming it; the partner guesses.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs throughout; hear three answers at the end, not thirty.

blocks.name: Home and where you live
blocks.language: *There is / there are*; prepositions; comparatives
steps: **Easier:** Where do you live? What is near your home? What is the best thing about your area? Do you prefer a city or the countryside?
**Harder:** What would you change about your town? Is it better to live where you grew up or to move away? What makes a place feel like home?
Give the comparative forms on the board if the class is A2.
After four questions, learners change partners and answer two of them again - better the second time.
blocks.variation: Learners draw their ideal home in two minutes and describe it to a partner.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Free time and weekends
blocks.language: Present simple; past simple; *enjoy / prefer* + -ing
steps: **Easier:** What do you do at the weekend? What did you do last Saturday? Do you prefer doing things alone or with other people?
**Harder:** Has the way people spend free time changed since your parents were young? Is being busy a good thing? What would you do with one completely free day?
Pairs first, then join two pairs and compare answers to the last question.
One learner from each four reports the most interesting answer.
blocks.variation: Rank five free-time activities and agree an order in the group of four.
blocks.bigClass: The join-into-fours step works with any class size; nobody presents from the front.

blocks.heading: People and experience (B1)
text: Personal but safe: nothing here asks a learner to reveal family or money troubles.

blocks.name: Friends
blocks.language: Present perfect; *know / meet*; adjectives of character
steps: **Easier:** How did you meet your best friend? What makes a good friend? How often do you see your friends?
**Harder:** Is it possible to be real friends with someone you have never met in person? Do friendships change when people move away? Can a friend be too honest?
Board four character adjectives before you start, and require one in every answer.
Pairs choose four questions; partner asks one follow-up each time.
blocks.variation: Each learner describes a friend without naming them; the class guesses whether they are older or younger.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Travel and journeys
blocks.language: Present perfect for experience; past simple for detail
steps: **Easier:** Have you ever travelled by train? What is the longest journey you have made? Where would you like to go?
**Harder:** Does travel really change people, or only the photographs they have? What is the difference between a traveller and a tourist? Should there be limits on flying?
Point out the pattern: the present perfect asks, the past simple answers - *Have you ever been to ...? Yes, I went in 2019.*
After four questions, change partners and retell one of your partner's answers.
blocks.variation: Plan a two-day trip for your partner based on what they said.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs; hear two retellings.

blocks.name: Learning English
blocks.language: *used to*; comparatives; *find it easy/hard to ...*
steps: **Easier:** How long have you studied English? What is easy for you? What is hard? Where do you use English outside class?
**Harder:** What is the fastest way to improve speaking? Does your first language help or get in the way? Should everyone learn a second language at school?
Collect the best advice on the board as a class list at the end - it becomes a poster for the room.
This set is worth doing in the first week of a course and again in the last.
blocks.variation: Learners write one piece of advice for a learner one level below them.
blocks.bigClass: The class list at the end is the whole-class stage; the talking stays in pairs.

blocks.heading: Opinions and ideas (B1 to B2)
text: For classes that can hold a position and give a reason. Safe subjects, real disagreement.

blocks.name: Technology and phones
blocks.language: *Should*; *would*; agreeing and disagreeing
steps: **Easier:** How long do you use your phone each day? What do you use it for most? Could you live without it for a week?
**Harder:** Should phones be allowed in schools? Has technology made people better at communicating, or worse? What should children not be allowed to do online?
Board three phrases for disagreeing politely: *I see your point, but ... That depends on ... I'm not so sure.*
Pairs discuss, then fours try to agree one answer to the second harder question.
blocks.variation: Take a vote before and after the discussion, and see whether anyone changed their mind.
blocks.bigClass: The fours stage needs no space and no presenting.

blocks.name: Work and jobs
blocks.language: Future forms; conditionals; job vocabulary
steps: **Easier:** What job would you like? What jobs are common in your area? What makes a job good?
**Harder:** Is it better to have work you love or work that pays well? Will people still do the same jobs in twenty years? Should everybody retire at the same age?
Avoid asking what learners' parents earn or do, which is not safe ground in every class.
Pairs choose four questions and must reach a conclusion, not just exchange views.
blocks.variation: Each pair invents a job that will exist in 2050 and explains it.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: School and learning
blocks.language: *Should*; passive forms; giving examples
steps: **Easier:** What is your favourite subject and why? What time does your school day start? What would you change about it?
**Harder:** Are exams a fair way to measure what someone knows? Should students choose all their own subjects? Is homework useful?
Require one example from experience in each answer: *For example, last year we ...*
Groups of three so that a quiet learner can enter the conversation more easily than in a four.
blocks.variation: Groups write one new school rule and argue for it.
blocks.bigClass: Threes work at once; take three conclusions.

blocks.heading: Imagination and hypotheticals (B1 to B2)
text: Conditionals in real use, and the questions learners remember after the lesson.

blocks.name: If you could choose
blocks.language: Second conditional; *would*; reasons
steps: **Easier:** If you could visit any country, where would you go? If you had one free day, what would you do? If you could learn one new skill, what?
**Harder:** If you could change one decision you have made, would you? If you had to live in another century, which would you choose? If you could know one thing about the future, would you want to?
Drill the form once: *If + past, would + verb*. Beginners tend to answer with *will*.
Partner must ask *why* after every answer - the reason is where the language is.
blocks.variation: Answer as somebody else - a grandparent, a famous person - and the partner guesses who.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Rules of a new country
blocks.language: *Must / mustn't*; *should*; obligation and permission
steps: Each group invents a small country and agrees five rules everyone must follow.
Two rules must be about school, and two about the environment.
Groups swap rules with another group and ask three hard questions about them.
Which country would the class prefer to live in?
blocks.variation: Each group also invents one rule that would be unpopular but useful.
blocks.bigClass: Swapping between neighbouring groups means nothing goes to the front.

blocks.name: Ten years from now
blocks.language: Future forms; *I hope to ...*; *I might ...*
steps: **Easier:** Where do you think you will live? What will you be doing? What will be the same?
**Harder:** What will have changed in your town? Will people read fewer books? What is one thing you hope will not change?
Teach the difference between *will* for prediction and *might* for possibility before they start.
Change partners once and report your first partner's answer to the new one.
blocks.variation: Write a two-sentence message to yourself in ten years, and read it to a partner.
blocks.bigClass: The change of partner works as "turn and face the row behind you".

items.title: Learners answer in one word and stop.
text: Two causes: the question had a yes/no answer, or they had no thinking time. Use questions that begin with *what, why, how*, give thirty seconds of silence first, and make the follow-up question a rule rather than a hope.

items.title: Can I use these with a mixed-level class?
text: That is why each set has easier and harder questions. Weaker pairs take the first group, stronger pairs the second, and the topic is the same across the room, so feedback at the end works for everybody.

items.title: Should I correct their English during a conversation?
text: No. Note what you hear and put four sentences on the board at the end for the class to repair, unnamed. Correcting mid-conversation teaches learners that speaking is dangerous.

items.title: How do I stop the confident ones dominating?
text: Give turns a shape: each learner answers one question fully before anyone answers a second; or in threes, one asks, one answers, one listens for the follow-up question and then swaps. Structure beats asking people to speak less.

items.title: How many questions should one lesson use?
text: Four, well answered, with follow-ups and a change of partner, is a better twenty minutes than twelve questions rushed.

pages.title: 15 ESL Listening Activities With No Recording Needed
pages.metaTitle: 15 ESL Listening Activities With No Recording Needed (A1-B2)
pages.description: 15 free ESL listening activities needing no recording or speakers: gist, detail, listening and doing, and listening to each other, with steps for each.
pages.keywords: ESL listening activities, listening activities without audio, teaching listening ESL, EFL listening tasks, dictogloss, picture dictation, listening for gist and detail
pages.teaches: Listening for gist, listening for detail, and listening to respond

hero.text: Fifteen listening activities that need no audio file, no speakers and no internet. The source is your own voice, or the learners' voices, which in most classrooms is the only source that works every day.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: They are grouped by what kind of listening they train: listening for the general idea, listening for exact information, listening and doing something physical, and listening to each other. Each one says what it practises, how long it takes and how to run it with forty learners.

blocks.heading: How to make a listening task work
bullets: **Set the task before you speak, not after.** A learner who knows what to listen for listens; a learner who hears "listen carefully" tries to hold everything and holds nothing. Put the question on the board first.
**Play it twice, and change the task between the two.** First listening for the general idea, second for detail. Two listenings with one task is a test; two listenings with two tasks is teaching.

**Speak naturally, then slow down the pauses, not the words.** Teachers who say each word separately remove exactly the features - linking, weak forms, contractions - that learners need to get used to. Keep normal speed and leave longer gaps between sentences.

**Let them compare answers in pairs before you check.** It takes thirty seconds, it doubles what they hear from the second listening, and it saves the learner who got nothing from having to say so in front of everyone.

**When they fail, find out why.** Did they not know the word, not catch it in the stream of speech, or not understand the question? Replay just that phrase and let them hear it again. "Listen more carefully" is not feedback.
**Difficulty lives in the task, not only in the text.** The same short story can be A2 ("how many people are in it?") or B2 ("why did she change her mind?"). Keep your texts and grade the questions.

blocks.heading: Listening for the general idea
text: The first thing a listener needs: what is this about, who is talking, and why. These come before any detail work.

blocks.name: The three-guess story
blocks.prep: None - think of a short true story from your week
blocks.language: Past simple narrative; any topic vocabulary
steps: Tell the class you will describe something that happened to you this week, and that they must decide *where* it happened. Write three places on the board as options.
Tell the story in six or seven sentences, at normal speed. Do not name the place.
Learners vote by raising hands, then tell a partner which words made them choose.
Tell the story again. This time they listen for one detail you changed - and there is one, so change it.
blocks.variation: Learners tell their own three-guess stories in groups of four while the others guess the place.
blocks.bigClass: Vote by standing under one of three signs taped to the walls. Thirty seconds, and you can see every answer.

blocks.name: Headline it
blocks.prep: None - two short news-style items you can say from memory
blocks.language: Present perfect and past simple; noun phrases
steps: Explain that a headline is short, has no unnecessary words, and says the main point.
Read a four-sentence news item twice. Pairs write a headline of six words or fewer.
Collect three or four headlines on the board and ask which one tells a reader the most. Do not rank them yourself - ask the class.
Repeat with the second item. Headlines get noticeably better the second time, which is the point.
blocks.variation: Give the headline first and ask learners to predict three things the item will mention. Then read it.
blocks.bigClass: One headline per pair on a slip of paper. Collect ten at random and read them out; the class chooses the clearest.

blocks.name: Two versions of the same day
blocks.language: Past simple; adjectives of feeling; time expressions
steps: Tell the class you will describe the same day twice: once as somebody who enjoyed it and once as somebody who did not.
Describe the day twice, five sentences each, without saying which version is which.
Learners decide which version was which and write down two words that told them - usually adjectives and the things each speaker chose to mention.
Draw out the idea that a speaker's attitude is carried by what they leave out as much as by what they say.
blocks.variation: At B2, use the same technique with an opinion: describe one change to the school from two points of view.
blocks.bigClass: Works unchanged - the pair discussion is the whole activity and needs no monitoring to be useful.

blocks.heading: Listening for exact information
text: Numbers, names, times and facts - the listening that everyday life and every examination asks for.

blocks.name: Five planted mistakes
blocks.prep: A short text you know well - the last reading text works
blocks.language: Whatever the text contains; excellent for recycling
steps: Learners close their books. Tell them you will read a text they know and change exactly five things.
Read at normal speed. Learners raise a hand or tap the desk each time they hear a change, and write what it should be.
In pairs they compare their five. Read once more so they can check the ones they argued about.
Ask which mistake was hardest to catch. It is almost always a small grammatical one rather than a wrong fact, and that is worth saying out loud.
blocks.variation: Learners prepare the five changes themselves and read to their group. They listen much harder when they have had to plant the mistakes.
blocks.bigClass: Tapping the desk beats hands up: you can hear the wave of recognition and see who is a beat behind.

blocks.name: Numbers, names and times
blocks.prep: None - improvise a message with eight pieces of information
blocks.language: Numbers, dates, times, spelling aloud, prices
steps: Learners draw a simple form: name, phone, date, time, place, price, two extras.
Say a telephone message once at normal speed, containing all eight. Include a correction - "sorry, that's the fourteenth, not the fourth" - because real messages do.
Say it a second time. Learners complete the form, then check in pairs.
Check the two items most classes get wrong: the corrected item and any number between thirteen and nineteen.
blocks.variation: Learners write their own messages and dictate to a partner, who must read the completed form back.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed. Project or draw the blank form on the board so nobody spends the listening time ruling lines.

blocks.name: Dictogloss in four steps
blocks.prep: A text of about sixty words at the class's level
blocks.language: Whatever grammar the text shows; excellent after a grammar lesson
steps: First reading: learners only listen, pens down, and get the general meaning.
Second reading at normal speed: learners write down the words they catch - single words, not sentences.
In groups of four, learners pool their words and rebuild the text so that it means the same and is grammatically correct. It does not have to be identical.
Groups compare their version with the original, on the board or read aloud. The discussion of the differences is where the grammar is learnt.
blocks.variation: Choose a text containing the structure you taught last lesson. The rebuilding forces them to use it and to notice when they have not.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of five or six work fine. One writer per group keeps the noise manageable; rotate the writer if you do this often.

blocks.name: Directions on a blank map
blocks.prep: Learners draw the grid themselves - no photocopying
blocks.language: Prepositions of place; directions; ordinal numbers
steps: Learners draw four horizontal and four vertical lines: a simple street grid. Mark one square "START".
Give directions aloud and name a building at the end: "Go up two streets, turn right, it's the second building on your left. That's the post office." Learners write the name in the square.
Give five or six such sets. Then learners compare maps in pairs and find where they diverged.
Ask two learners with different maps to explain their route. The class decides who followed the instructions.
blocks.variation: Learners give the directions in pairs, back to back, with one describing and one drawing.
blocks.bigClass: Perfect for large classes - everybody has a pen and paper, and pair-checking finds the errors without you.

blocks.heading: Listening and doing
text: Listening checked by an action rather than an answer - the fastest way to see who understood, and the best for young learners and mixed levels.

blocks.name: Picture dictation
blocks.language: Prepositions of place; there is and there are; any object vocabulary
steps: Learners take a blank half-page. Warn them that drawing quality does not matter and will not be commented on.
Describe a simple scene in eight sentences: "There's a tree on the left. There are three birds above the tree." Pause after each.
Learners compare drawings in pairs and find the differences, then say which sentence caused each one.
Draw or describe the original and let them check. Keep the sentences, not the picture - you will use them again.
blocks.variation: At B1, describe the scene once at normal speed with no pauses, then again with pauses. The contrast teaches them something about their own listening.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed. Learners who finish early add one thing you did not mention and challenge their partner to find it.

blocks.name: Listen and build
blocks.prep: None - one sheet of paper each
blocks.language: Sequencing and instructions: first, then, next, fold, turn over, press
steps: Everybody takes one sheet of paper. Give folding instructions step by step, without showing anything: "Fold it in half, long side to long side."
Make no corrections and answer no questions for the first four steps - learners must listen rather than copy their neighbour.
After six steps, hold up your own paper. Learners compare and work out which instruction lost them.
Do it once more, faster, with learners giving the instructions.
blocks.variation: Instead of folding, learners arrange six objects from their bag on the desk in the order and position you describe.
blocks.bigClass: Ideal: silent, visible, and you can see every learner's result from the front in one glance.

blocks.name: Minimal pair corners
blocks.prep: None - choose the pair your learners confuse
blocks.language: Pronunciation: ship and sheep, walk and work, sit and seat
steps: Write one word on the left of the board and one on the right. Say each three times so the class hears the difference before being asked to judge it.
Learners point left or right as you say a word at random. Keep it fast, ten or twelve words.
Include the same word twice in a row. It stops them guessing by alternation, which is how half of them survive this activity.
Then reverse it: a learner says a word and the class points. This is the harder half and the more useful one.
blocks.variation: Put the two words in sentences - "I can see a ship / I can see a sheep" - so learners judge them in the stream of speech, where it actually matters.
blocks.bigClass: Pointing works at any class size. Watch the back rows: they copy the front rows, so call words with your back turned occasionally.

blocks.name: Shadowing the teacher
blocks.prep: Four or five sentences from a text they have read
blocks.language: Stress, rhythm, linking and weak forms
steps: Read one sentence at natural speed. Learners listen only.
Read it again; learners speak along with you, half a word behind, quietly. Tell them to copy the rhythm even if they lose some words.
Read it a third time; learners say it with you at full volume. Then they say it alone.
Ask what was hardest. It is usually the unstressed words they had not noticed were unstressed.
blocks.variation: Record nothing and demonstrate nothing else: shadow the same sentences at the start of five lessons and the change in rhythm is audible.
blocks.bigClass: Better in a large class than a small one - nobody is exposed, and the whole room carries the rhythm.

blocks.heading: Listening to each other
text: The listening learners will do most of, and the listening classrooms practise least. These activities make not listening impossible.

blocks.name: The missing half
blocks.prep: Two short sets of information - a timetable, a price list, a family
blocks.language: Question forms; asking for repetition; numbers
steps: Give learner A half the information and learner B the other half. Neither may look at the other's paper.
Teach the three phrases they will need first: *Sorry, could you say that again? Do you mean ...? How do you spell that?*
Pairs complete their own sheet by asking. Nothing may be shown or passed.
Compare sheets at the end. Where the information is wrong, ask what happened - almost always a number or a name that was said once and not checked.
blocks.variation: Sit pairs back to back. It removes lip-reading and gesture, and the asking-for-repetition phrases suddenly get used.
blocks.bigClass: Write both halves on the board's two ends before the lesson, have learners copy one half, then pair them across the aisle.

blocks.name: The note-taker's summary
blocks.language: Reported speech; summarising; agreeing and disagreeing
steps: In each group of three, two learners discuss a question for three minutes while the third takes notes and says nothing.
The note-taker then summarises what each speaker said, in reported speech: "Nimal said he thought ..., but Ayesha disagreed because ..."
The two speakers correct the summary where it misrepresents them. This correction is the most useful minute in the activity.
Rotate so all three take a turn as note-taker.
blocks.variation: The note-taker may not write full sentences, only five words in total. Summarising from five words forces real listening.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of three are ideal in a crowded room; nobody needs to move, and the volume stays low because only two talk at a time.

blocks.name: Whose weekend was it?
blocks.language: Past simple; listening for detail; question forms
steps: Each learner writes three sentences about their weekend on an unsigned slip of paper.
Collect the slips within each group and redistribute. One learner reads a slip aloud, twice.
The group guesses whose weekend it was and must give one reason from what they heard.
The writer confirms and adds one sentence they did not write down. The group asks two follow-up questions.
blocks.variation: Slips describe a future plan instead, and the group guesses using *will* and *going to*.
blocks.bigClass: Keep the slips inside each group - collecting for the whole class takes five minutes and gains nothing.

blocks.name: One fact before you speak
blocks.language: Reported speech; linking words; any discussion topic
steps: Set a question the group will discuss - a real one, on which they will disagree.
The rule: before saying anything of your own, you must repeat one thing the previous speaker said. "You said the bus is cheaper. I think ..."
Run the discussion for five minutes. Enforce the rule strictly for the first two - the activity collapses without it.
Afterwards, ask how the discussion was different. Learners usually say it was slower, which it is, and that they remembered more, which is the point.
blocks.variation: At B2, the repetition must be a paraphrase, not the speaker's own words.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of six with one learner as rule-keeper. The rule-keeper role is a gift to the learner who never speaks.

blocks.heading: In short
text: None of these need equipment, which means none of them can fail because the speakers do not work. What they do need is a task set before you speak and a second listening with a different question.
If you use recordings as well, the same principles apply: task first, twice with two questions, pair-check before whole-class checking, and when they fail, find out which of the three reasons it was.

items.title: Can I really teach listening without recordings?
text: You can teach most of it. Your own voice gives learners a real speaker who links words, uses weak forms and repairs himself, and you can repeat any phrase instantly, which no audio file allows. What your voice cannot give is other accents and other voices, so use recordings for that when you have them - and the activities on this page still work around them.

items.title: My learners say they understand nothing at natural speed.
text: Then the task is too hard, not the speed. Keep the speed and ask for less: how many speakers, happy or angry, one number. Slowing your speech teaches learners to understand speech nobody outside the classroom produces.

items.title: How many times should I play or read a text?
text: Twice as standard, with a different task each time, and a third time for the one phrase they argued about. More than three full listenings and they stop listening and start remembering.

items.title: Should learners see the text afterwards?
text: Yes, at the end. Reading the text after listening is where a learner discovers that the word they could not catch was one they already knew - and that is the moment that improves their listening, not the score.

items.title: What do I do about the learners who never listen to each other?
text: Make not listening impossible rather than asking for it: One fact before you speak, The note-taker's summary and The missing half all break down immediately if somebody has not listened, and learners feel that themselves.

pages.title: 15 ESL Role-Play Activities With Role Cards
pages.metaTitle: 15 ESL Role-Play Activities With Role Cards (A1-B2)
pages.description: 15 free ESL role-plays with both roles written out: shops, work, problems to solve and disagreements, each with the language it needs and a class note.
pages.keywords: ESL role play activities, role play cards ESL, English role plays for adults, functional language role play, ESL speaking role plays, role play ideas for English class
pages.teaches: Functional language, fluency and dealing with the unexpected in speech

hero.text: Fifteen role-plays with the roles written out, ready to copy onto the board or onto slips of paper. Each one says what language it practises, how long it takes, and what each partner knows that the other does not.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: They are grouped by what they are for: everyday transactions, work and study, situations with a problem to solve, and role-plays where learners disagree. The last group is the one that produces real fluency, and the one most classes never reach.

blocks.heading: What makes a role-play work rather than die
bullets: **Give each partner different information.** A role-play where both learners know everything is a conversation about nothing. A's card should contain something B's does not - a price, a time, a reason, a refusal.

**Put the functional language on the board and leave it there.** *Could you tell me ...? I'm afraid that won't be possible. Would you mind if ...?* Learners cannot invent these while also inventing what to say.
**Give a minute to read the card and think, in silence.** Learners who start speaking immediately produce their first idea and stop. A minute of thinking time roughly doubles what a pair produces.
**Never start with a performance.** Everyone does the role-play at the same time, in pairs. If you want it heard, hear one pair at the end, after they have already done it once.
**Swap roles and run it a second time.** The second run is the fluent one, and it costs three minutes. This single habit does more for fluency than any new activity.
**Do not correct during the role-play.** Write down four sentences you hear, two correct and two not, and put them on the board unnamed afterwards for the class to sort out.

**Keep the roles close to the learners' lives.** A learner who has never been in a bank plays a bank clerk badly. A learner playing an angry customer at a phone shop has the vocabulary and the feeling already.

blocks.heading: Everyday transactions
text: Short, repeatable and useful outside the classroom. Best at A1 to A2, and good as five-minute warmers at any level.

blocks.name: At the ticket counter
blocks.prep: Write both roles on the board
blocks.language: Asking for information; times and prices; *How much is ...? What time does it leave?*
steps: Role A (traveller): you want to go to the nearest big city tomorrow morning, arriving before ten. You have 800 rupees. Find out the time, the price and the platform.
Role B (clerk): the morning trains leave at 5.40, 7.15 and 9.30. The 7.15 is full. Tickets cost 620 for the express and 310 for the slow train, which takes two hours longer. Platform 3.
Give a minute of silent reading, then run it in pairs simultaneously. Everybody speaks at once.
Swap roles and run it again with the traveller now needing to arrive before eight - which makes the only option the slow train.
blocks.variation: Role B may not simply read out the timetable: the clerk answers only what is asked, so A has to ask three questions properly.
blocks.bigClass: Both roles on the board, left half and right half. Rows work in pairs without anyone moving.

blocks.name: Returning something that does not work
blocks.prep: Role cards, or both roles on the board
blocks.language: Complaining politely; *It doesn't work. I'd like a refund. Do you have the receipt?*
steps: Role A (customer): you bought a phone charger four days ago. It worked for two days. You want your money back, not another charger. You have lost the receipt but you paid by card.
Role B (shop assistant): without a receipt you can normally only exchange, not refund. You may make an exception if the customer can show the card payment. You must not lose the customer.
Teach three phrases first: *I'm afraid ... , Would you be able to ... , Let me see what I can do.*
Run it in pairs. At the end ask how many customers got a refund and how they managed it - that discussion is where the polite-complaint language is noticed.
blocks.variation: At B1, A has no card record either, and B must refuse without losing the customer. Much harder, and much more useful.
blocks.bigClass: No change. Ask three pairs to report the outcome in one sentence rather than acting it out.

blocks.name: Ordering for somebody with a problem
blocks.language: Food vocabulary; requests and modifications; *Does it contain ...? Could we have it without ...?*
steps: Two learners are customers and the third is the waiter. One customer cannot eat something - dairy, nuts, chilli - and does not know the menu.
The waiter invents the menu as they go, which is the point: it forces real listening and real questions.
The customers must order two courses that are safe for both, and ask at least two questions about ingredients.
Rotate the waiter and run it twice more so everybody takes the harder role.
blocks.variation: The waiter's restaurant has run out of two things, and only says so when they are ordered.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of three suit a crowded room - nobody moves and only one learner speaks at a time within each group.

blocks.heading: Work and study
text: The role-plays adult learners most often say they need. Best at B1 and above.

blocks.name: Hiring for the hotel
blocks.language: Present perfect for experience; talking about strengths; hedging: *I'd say ... , I tend to ...*
steps: Role A (candidate): you are applying to be a receptionist at a hotel. You are good with people and you speak three languages. You have never used a computer booking system.
Role B (interviewer): you need somebody who can start next week and use the booking system from day one. Ask about experience, languages, and one weakness.
Put four interview questions on the board and teach two hedging phrases for the weakness question.
Swap roles with a different job - a delivery driver with no licence yet - so the second run is not a repeat.
blocks.variation: The interviewer must decide yes or no at the end and give one reason. Candidates take the reason far more seriously than a mark.
blocks.bigClass: Works as it stands. Collect the yes or no decisions with a show of hands - it takes twenty seconds and gives the class a result.

blocks.name: Asking for time off
blocks.language: Requests and refusals; reasons; *I was wondering whether ... , The problem is ...*
steps: Role A (employee): you need three days off next week for a family wedding. You already took two days last month. You are willing to work the following Saturday.
Role B (manager): two other people are already away next week. You can allow one day, or three if the employee finds somebody to cover.
Teach the structure of the request: reason, request, offer. Then teach one phrase for a soft refusal.
Run it, swap, and run it again with the manager now unable to agree to anything - so A has to accept a refusal politely, which is the harder skill.
blocks.variation: At B2, the manager must say no and keep the employee willing. Both learners then report the conversation to a third learner in reported speech.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Explaining the missed deadline
blocks.language: Past simple and past continuous; apologising; *I should have ... , What happened was ...*
steps: Role A (student or junior colleague): your work is two days late. The real reason is that you misunderstood what was wanted and started again on Monday.
Role B (teacher or manager): you want the work, an explanation, and a new date you can trust. You do not want an apology repeated four times.
Teach the shape of a useful explanation: what happened, what you did about it, when it will be ready. Not three apologies.
Swap roles. The second time, B has already had this conversation with A once before.
blocks.variation: A must not use the word *sorry* more than once. It forces them into the language that actually repairs the situation.
blocks.bigClass: No change. Two pairs may report the agreed new deadline; that is enough feedback.

blocks.name: The parents' evening
blocks.language: Describing progress; giving advice; softening bad news
steps: Role A (teacher): the learner works hard in class and does almost no homework. Marks are falling.
Role B (parent): you believe two hours of homework are done every evening. You want to know why the marks are falling.
Role C (the learner): you are present. You do homework with your phone beside you and it takes four hours to do one hour's work.
Run the three-way conversation, then ask each group what they agreed. Groups almost always arrive at the phone, which makes the language of advice necessary rather than an exercise.
blocks.variation: Role C says nothing for the first two minutes. The two adults must then ask questions rather than talk about the learner.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of three are the easiest grouping in a crowded room; write the three roles in three columns on the board.

blocks.heading: Situations with a problem to solve
text: Role-plays where the pair has to reach an outcome. The outcome is what keeps the talk going past the first two turns.

blocks.name: The lost luggage
blocks.language: Describing objects; past simple; insisting politely; *Are you sure ...? Could you check again?*
steps: Role A (traveller): your bag did not arrive. It is dark blue, has a red ribbon on the handle, and contains medicine you need tonight.
Role B (airline staff): the computer shows no bag matching that description. You can offer 5,000 rupees and delivery tomorrow, but nothing tonight.
Teach two phrases for insisting without rudeness, and one for the staff member holding a line.
Run it, swap roles, and run it again with the medicine detail removed so the pair notice how much the urgency changed the conversation.
blocks.variation: Role B speaks first and offers the money immediately. A has to refuse an offer and keep asking, which is harder than complaining.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: The neighbour's noise
blocks.language: Complaining to somebody you will meet again; *I don't want to make a problem, but ... , Would it be possible to ...?*
steps: Role A: your neighbour's music keeps your family awake three nights a week. You have to live beside this person for years.
Role B: you work nights and practise music in the evening because it is the only time you have. You did not know anyone could hear it.
Put on the board the difference between a complaint that ends a relationship and one that fixes a problem, and three phrases for the second kind.
Run it and ask each pair for the agreement they reached. Compare two very different agreements with the class.
blocks.variation: A has already complained twice and nothing changed. The language needed changes completely, and learners feel that.
blocks.bigClass: No change. The agreements can be collected in one word each - *time limit, headphones, weekends* - and written on the board.

blocks.name: One room, two bookings
blocks.language: Negotiating; apologising; offering alternatives; *What if we ...? That's not really acceptable.*
steps: Two guests have bookings for the same last room; the third learner is the hotel receptionist.
Guest A booked first and has a confirmation. Guest B arrived first, is already unpacked, and has a small child.
The receptionist has one room in a hotel twenty minutes away and a discount to offer, and must not lose either guest's goodwill.
Every group must reach a decision. Compare solutions at the end - there are usually four or five, which is the interesting part.
blocks.variation: The receptionist may not offer the other hotel for the first three minutes.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of three; the comparison of solutions at the end works better with a big class than a small one.

blocks.name: Borrowing what you broke
blocks.language: Admitting; offering to repair; *I'm afraid I've ... , Let me pay for it.*
steps: Role A: you borrowed a friend's bicycle and bent the wheel. You cannot afford a new one this month.
Role B: you need the bicycle to get to work on Monday. You lent it because you were asked nicely, and this is the second time.
Teach three ways of admitting something that are neither a confession nor an excuse, and one way of offering a solution instead of an apology.
Run it, then swap so that everybody has to both admit and be annoyed.
blocks.variation: Role A must open the conversation with the bad news in the first sentence. Learners find that hard, and it is precisely the useful bit.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.heading: Role-plays where learners disagree
text: The group most classes never reach, and the one that produces real fluency: two roles that cannot both get what they want. Best at B1 and B2.

blocks.name: The family car
blocks.language: Agreeing and disagreeing; making a case; conceding; *You've got a point, but ...*
steps: The family has one car and four people want it on Saturday: for a job interview, for a sick relative's hospital visit, to move furniture, and for a football match that has been paid for.
Each learner gets one role and one minute to prepare their case. They may not see the other roles.
The group must reach a decision everybody can live with within eight minutes, and the decision cannot be *take turns*.
Each group reports its decision and one reason. Different groups decide differently, which is the discussion the class then has.
blocks.variation: Give one learner the deciding vote. The language changes from arguing to persuading, and the difference is worth naming.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of four in a fixed-desk room: two learners turn round. Nothing else is needed.

blocks.name: Cutting one thing from the budget
blocks.language: Presenting a case; refusing; compromising; comparatives and superlatives
steps: The school must cut one of four things: the library, the sports programme, the computer room, or the school bus.
Each learner represents one of them and has a minute to prepare two reasons why theirs must stay.
The group must agree on one cut. Nobody may defend more than one thing, and everybody must speak before the decision.
Collect the decisions. Ask the groups who cut the bus whether anybody in the group actually takes it - the answer usually makes a point about arguing from your own position.
blocks.variation: At B2, add a fifth role with no stake and the final say. That learner has to summarise both sides fairly before deciding.
blocks.bigClass: Ideal for a large class: four learners per group, no movement, and a result from every group in one word.

blocks.name: The rule nobody likes
blocks.language: Modals of obligation; making and refusing requests; *We're not allowed to ... , Why can't we ...?*
steps: Role A (learner representative): you want the rule about phones changed. You have forty signatures.
Role B (teacher or principal): the rule exists because last year two examinations had to be cancelled. You are willing to discuss a limited change, not removal.
Teach the language of a proposal - *We'd like to suggest ... , On condition that ...* - and the language of a conditional yes.
Run it, swap roles, and ask what changes were actually agreed. Realistic proposals succeed and total demands fail, which learners notice without being told.
blocks.variation: Role A may not mention the phone directly for the first minute and must open with the problem it causes.
blocks.bigClass: No change. Collect the agreed changes on the board and let the class vote on the best proposal.

blocks.name: Two witnesses, one accident
blocks.language: Past continuous and past simple; contradicting politely; reported speech
steps: Two learners witnessed the same minor accident and each gets a short account that contradicts the other on three points: the colour of the vehicle, the speed, and who was on the phone.
The third learner is the insurance officer, who must question both and then write three agreed facts and three disputed ones.
Witnesses must not see each other's accounts, and neither is lying - each simply saw part of it.
The officer reports the findings to the class in reported speech: *He said the car was ... , but she claimed ...*
blocks.variation: Add a fourth role: the driver, who arrives at the end and hears the report. The driver may object twice.
blocks.bigClass: Write the two accounts on the two sides of the board before the lesson and have each witness copy only their own.

blocks.heading: In short
text: The pattern under all fifteen is the same: different information for each partner, the functional language on the board, thinking time in silence, everybody at once, and a second run with the roles swapped.

Change the situations to suit your learners - the local bus station, the shop on their street, their own school's rules. A role-play about a place learners know produces twice the language of one set in a country they have never visited.

items.title: My learners refuse to act. What then?
text: Do not ask them to act. A role-play is not drama: nobody stands up, nobody performs, everybody stays in their seat and talks to the person beside them. Most refusal is a fear of performing in front of the class, and that fear disappears when all twenty pairs speak at once.

items.title: Do I need printed role cards?
text: No. Both roles written on the two halves of the board works for everything on this page, and for many role-plays it is better - learners look up and read rather than hiding behind paper. Print cards only when the two roles must not be seen by the other partner.

items.title: How do I stop one partner doing all the talking?
text: Give the quieter role the information the other one needs. If A must find out three things that only B knows, B has to speak. An imbalance in a role-play is nearly always an imbalance in the information.

items.title: Should I correct their mistakes?
text: Not during the role-play - correction stops fluency and the stopping is what learners remember. Note four sentences, two right and two wrong, and put them on the board unnamed at the end for the class to sort out.

items.title: Is a role-play worth the time if the examination is written?
text: Yes. Learners who have argued a case aloud write that argument faster and with better structure, and the functional language - requests, refusals, proposals - is the same language written examinations ask for in letters and emails.

items.title: How do I use these online?
text: Two learners per breakout room, the roles pasted into the chat, and one sentence typed into the main chat at the end saying what was agreed. The written outcome is what tells you the conversation happened.

pages.title: 20 ESL Speaking Activities for Beginners
pages.metaTitle: 20 ESL Speaking Activities for Beginners (A1-A2)
pages.description: 20 speaking activities for A1-A2 ESL classes: the language each one practises, numbered steps, a variation, and a note for classes of 40 or more.
pages.keywords: ESL speaking activities for beginners, A1 speaking activities, A2 speaking practice, EFL speaking activities for large classes, getting beginners to speak English
pages.teaches: Speaking fluency at beginner level

hero.text: Twenty speaking activities for A1 and A2 classes, each with the language it practises, numbered steps, a variation and a note for large classes. Most need nothing but the learners themselves.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: They are grouped by what they are for: quick warmers, pair work, whole-class mingles, and longer tasks for the end of a lesson. Every one has been written so that you can run it straight from this page.

blocks.heading: Running speaking with beginners
bullets: **Model it first, then check.** Do the activity once with a strong learner in front of the class, then ask an instruction-checking question: *Do you write, or do you speak?* *Do you ask one question or two?* A beginner class goes silent far more often from not understanding the task than from not knowing the English.
**Give the language before the task, not during it.** Put the two or three question forms on the board and drill them once. Beginners cannot invent *Did you go ...?* while also thinking what to say.
**Let them plan quietly.** Thirty seconds to think, or to write three words, doubles what most beginners say. Notes, not sentences.
**Do not correct while they speak.** Write down two or three mistakes you hear and deal with them afterwards, on the board, without naming anyone.
**Expect some first language, and set a limit rather than a ban.** "English only for these three minutes" works; "never use your language" does not.
**Change partners.** The same two learners talking every lesson stop listening to each other. Move one row along, or one line rotates.

blocks.heading: Quick warmers: five minutes or less
text: For the first minutes of a lesson, to get everyone speaking before anything else happens.

blocks.name: Two truths and one lie
blocks.language: Present simple and past simple statements; *Is that true?*
steps: Say three sentences about yourself. Two are true, one is not: *I have two sisters. I lived in another country. I can drive.*
The class guesses the false one and you tell them.
Learners write three sentences about themselves, one false.
In pairs, they read their sentences and guess. Each guess needs a reason: *I think number two is false because ...*
blocks.variation: For A1, give the three sentence frames on the board: *I have ..., I can ..., I like ...*
blocks.bigClass: Keep it in pairs, then ask three or four learners to tell the class one sentence and let the class vote by hands.

blocks.name: Three words about yesterday
blocks.language: Past simple; time expressions
steps: Write three words on the board about your own yesterday: *bus, rice, phone.*
Tell the class the three sentences behind them: *I took the bus to school. I cooked rice. I lost my phone!*
Learners write three words about their yesterday - words only.
In pairs, they swap papers, guess the story behind their partner's words, then hear the real one.
blocks.variation: Use last weekend, or last holiday, for more to talk about.
blocks.bigClass: Works as it stands: everyone speaks at once in pairs. Collect two or three stories at the end.

blocks.name: Stand up if
blocks.language: Present simple questions; short answers
steps: Say a sentence: *Stand up if you walked to school today.* Everyone it is true for stands up.
Ask one standing learner a follow-up question: *How long does it take?*
After three or four of yours, learners take over and say their own *Stand up if ...* sentences.
blocks.variation: For classes that cannot move, learners raise a hand or hold up a pen.
blocks.bigClass: Better with a big class than a small one: you see the whole room answer at once.

blocks.name: The question ball
blocks.prep: A soft ball, or a rolled-up paper ball
blocks.language: Wh- questions; personal information
steps: Put six question words on the board: *What, Where, When, Who, Why, How.*
Throw the ball to a learner and say a question word. They make a question with it and ask any classmate.
That classmate answers, then throws the ball on and says a new question word.
blocks.variation: Name a topic as well as the word - *Where ... food* - so questions stay on one subject.
blocks.bigClass: Throw only within one half of the room, then swap halves; or pass the ball hand to hand along rows.

blocks.name: Countdown from ten
blocks.language: Fluency: any known language, spoken without stopping
steps: Give a very easy topic: *your family, your street, food you like.*
Learner A speaks for ten seconds without stopping. Then B does the same.
Repeat the same topic for eight seconds, then six. The aim is to say the same things faster and more easily, not to say more.
blocks.variation: Let learners choose the topic from three you write on the board.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed. Time the whole class at once with your watch.

blocks.heading: Pair work: ten minutes
text: Every learner speaking for half the time, with a clear task and an end point.

blocks.name: Spot the six differences
blocks.prep: Two similar pictures, one for each learner in a pair
blocks.language: *There is / there are*; prepositions of place; *Has your picture got ...?*
steps: Give A picture one and B picture two. They must not look at each other's picture.
Put the language on the board: *In my picture there is ... Is there a ... in your picture?*
Pairs find the differences by speaking only - no pointing, no showing.
Check as a class: which pair found all six?
blocks.variation: Draw two simple scenes on the board yourself, show one half of the class each, then rub them out.
blocks.bigClass: Two pictures serve the whole room: rows one and three get picture A, rows two and four picture B.

blocks.name: Interview and report
blocks.language: Questions and short answers; third person *-s* in the report
steps: Learners write four questions about free time: *What do you do on Sunday?*
In pairs, they ask and answer, and write short notes.
Change partners. Each learner now tells the new partner about the first one: *Nadia plays volleyball on Sunday.*
Two or three report to the class.
blocks.variation: Give the four question stems for A1 classes, and let them add a fifth of their own.
blocks.bigClass: For the change of partner, one row stands and moves one place along; the last learner walks to the front.

blocks.name: What is in the bag?
blocks.prep: A bag with five or six ordinary objects
blocks.language: Adjectives; *It's made of ...*; *Is it heavy? Can you eat it?*
steps: Hold up the closed bag. Learners ask yes/no questions to guess one object: *Is it small? Is it plastic?*
Answer only *yes* or *no* until someone guesses.
Then pairs play the same game: each learner thinks of an object in their own bag or pocket, and the partner asks up to ten questions.
blocks.variation: No bag needed: learners think of any object in the classroom.
blocks.bigClass: Do one round with the class, then let every pair play at once; you do not need to hear them all.

blocks.name: The shop
blocks.prep: None, or price labels on the board
blocks.language: *How much is ...? I'd like ... Have you got ...?*; numbers and money
steps: Build the dialogue on the board with the class, line by line: greeting, request, price, payment, thanks.
Practise it once all together, then in pairs, reading.
Rub out five words and practise again. Rub out five more, and again, until most of the board is empty.
Pairs swap roles and change what they buy.
blocks.variation: Change the shop to a café, a ticket office or a pharmacy, and the class builds a new dialogue with the same shape.
blocks.bigClass: Rubbing out from the board suits any class size, because the whole room works from one text.

blocks.name: Ordering the day
blocks.language: Daily routine verbs; *first, then, after that, finally*
steps: Learners write six things they did yesterday, in any order, as short notes.
They swap papers. The partner must put the six in the right order by asking: *Did you have breakfast before you left home?*
The owner answers only *yes* or *no*.
Check: did the partner get the order right?
blocks.variation: For A1, give six verbs everyone uses: *get up, eat, go, study, play, sleep.*
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.heading: Whole-class mingles: everyone moving
text: For practising one question form many times, with many partners.

blocks.name: Find someone who
blocks.language: Yes/no questions; short answers; one follow-up question
steps: Write six prompts: *Find someone who ... walks to school / has a brother / can swim / watched television last night / likes mangoes / got up before six.*
Model the question: *Do you walk to school?* - *Yes, I do. / No, I don't.* Only a *yes* lets them write the name.
Add the rule: after a *yes*, ask one more question and remember the answer.
Learners find a different name for each prompt, then tell the class one thing they learned.
blocks.variation: Past simple version: *Find someone who cooked yesterday.*
blocks.bigClass: Rows instead of a mingle: ask the four people nearest you, then everybody moves one seat to the left.

blocks.name: Speed meeting
blocks.language: Personal information questions; repetition builds fluency
steps: Two lines face each other. Every learner has a partner opposite.
Give a question or topic: *your family.* They have 45 seconds to talk.
Call *change*. One line moves one place along; the learner at the end walks to the other end.
New topic, 45 seconds. Repeat four or five times.
blocks.variation: Keep the same topic for three changes: learners notice they say it better and faster each time.
blocks.bigClass: Make four short lines instead of two long ones, in the aisles or around the desks.

blocks.name: Class survey
blocks.language: One question form, many times; numbers and simple results
steps: Each learner chooses one question: *How do you come to school? What do you eat for breakfast?*
They ask ten classmates and keep a tally.
They write one sentence of result: *Seven of ten learners come by bus.*
Each learner reads their sentence to the class; you build a simple table on the board.
blocks.variation: Groups of four take one question each, then combine their results.
blocks.bigClass: Ask ten people within two rows, not across the whole room.

blocks.name: Guess my classmate
blocks.language: Present simple descriptions; *He/She has got ...*; clothes and appearance
steps: Each learner secretly chooses a classmate and writes three sentences about them, without the name: *She has got long hair. She sits near the window. She likes football.*
One learner reads their sentences.
The class guesses. The learner who guesses right reads next.
blocks.variation: Use famous people or characters the whole class knows, if pointing at classmates would be unkind in your class.
blocks.bigClass: Play in groups of six so that everyone gets a turn in the same ten minutes.

blocks.name: The chain story
blocks.language: Past simple; sequencing words
steps: Give the first line: *Yesterday, Rafa found a bag on the bus.*
Each learner in the group adds one sentence, going round the circle.
The story stops after two rounds, and the last speaker must end it.
One group tells the class their story.
blocks.variation: Write six words on the board that must appear somewhere in the story.
blocks.bigClass: Groups work at the same time without you listening to each; ask two groups to report.

blocks.heading: Longer tasks: fifteen minutes and up
text: For the end of a lesson, when learners have the language and need to use it for something.

blocks.name: Plan a day out
blocks.language: *Let's ... / Shall we ...?*; agreeing and disagreeing; times and places
steps: Each group plans one day out together with a small budget you set.
Give the language for agreeing: *Good idea. I think so too. I'm not sure.*
Groups decide where to go, when to meet and what to take, and write six lines of plan.
Each group tells the class its plan; the class votes for the best day out.
blocks.variation: Plan a class party, a school trip or a welcome day for a new student.
blocks.bigClass: Only three or four groups present; the rest hand in their plans or display them on the wall.

blocks.name: My photograph
blocks.prep: Learners need a photograph on their phone, or they draw one
blocks.language: Present continuous; past simple; *in this photo ...*
steps: Learners choose one photograph and think about three things: who is in it, where it was, why they keep it.
In pairs, each describes their photo for one minute while the partner listens without speaking.
The partner then asks three questions.
Two or three learners describe their photo to the class.
blocks.variation: No phones: learners draw a simple picture of a place they remember.
blocks.bigClass: Keep it in pairs; hear three volunteers at the end.

blocks.name: The alibi
blocks.language: Past simple questions and answers; times
steps: Two learners leave the room, or turn away, and agree a story: where they were together yesterday evening, from six to eight, and what they did.
The class prepares questions: *What time did you arrive? What did you eat?*
The two are questioned separately. The class listens for differences between the two stories.
Did the stories match? If not, where?
blocks.variation: For A1, limit the questions to five, and give them on the board.
blocks.bigClass: Run it in groups of six: two make the story, four ask. Every group plays at the same time.

blocks.name: Show and tell in sixty seconds
blocks.prep: Learners bring one small object, or use something they have
blocks.language: Describing; explaining why something matters
steps: Each learner has sixty seconds to show one object and say three things: what it is, where it came from, why they keep it.
Give two minutes of quiet preparation time and allow three words of notes only.
In groups of four, each takes a turn; the group asks one question each afterwards.
blocks.variation: Everyone speaks about the same kind of thing - a photo, a coin, a key - so the class hears the language many times.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of four, all at once: twenty-four learners all speak within ten minutes.

blocks.name: The job interview
blocks.language: *Can you ...? Do you like ...?*; abilities and simple experience
steps: The class invents one simple job together and lists four things the worker must be able to do.
In pairs, one is the manager and one the applicant. The manager asks about the four things.
Swap roles and change one thing about the job.
Each manager says whether they would give the applicant the job, and why.
blocks.variation: Choose a job the class finds funny - a dog walker, an ice-cream taster - to keep it light.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed: every pair works at the same time.

items.title: What if the class will not speak at all?
text: Start with pairs, not the whole class: a learner who will not speak in front of thirty will speak to the person next to them. Give thinking time first, and make the first activity one where the right answer cannot be wrong, such as Two truths and one lie.

items.title: How do I stop them using their own language?
text: Set a short limit - three minutes of English - rather than a rule for the whole lesson, and give the English they need on the board before they start. A beginner switching languages is usually missing a word, not being lazy.

items.title: Should I correct mistakes while they are speaking?
text: No. Note two or three mistakes and put them on the board afterwards, unnamed, for the class to correct together. Correcting during the task stops the speaking, which is the thing you are trying to build.

items.title: My class has fifty learners. Which of these still work?
text: All of them. Every activity above has a line for large classes: most turn into pair work done by everyone at once, with two or three pairs reporting at the end. You do not have to hear every learner to make the activity worth doing.
