pages.title: 20 ESL Speaking Activities for Teenagers
pages.metaTitle: 20 ESL Speaking Activities for Teenagers (A2-B1)
pages.description: 20 speaking activities for A2-B1 ESL classes: the language each one practises, numbered steps, a variation, and a note for classes of 40 or more.
pages.keywords: ESL speaking activities for teenagers, speaking activities for teens English class, EFL activities for secondary school, discussion activities for teenagers, B1 speaking activities
pages.teaches: Speaking fluency with teenage classes

hero.text: Twenty speaking activities that work with teenagers: competitive where competition helps, safe where a teenager would rather die than look foolish, and short enough to hold a class that has already had five lessons that day.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: Each activity gives the language it practises, numbered steps, a variation and a note for large classes. Most need nothing at all.

blocks.heading: What is different about a teenage class
bullets: **Fear of looking foolish beats willingness to try.** A teenager who would happily answer you alone will say nothing in front of thirty classmates. Almost everything here starts in pairs or small groups, where the audience is two people, not the room.

**Give them something to hide behind.** A role, a card, a character, a team - anything that means a mistake belongs to the part and not to them personally. It is the single most useful trick with this age group.
**Competition works, but keep it short and team-based.** Individual competition in front of the class humiliates the weakest learner; team competition over three minutes energises everyone.

**Their own lives are the best content, on their terms.** Music, food, phones, sport, what they would change about school. Avoid anything that forces a teenager to reveal family circumstances or money.
**Set a visible time limit.** "Three minutes" written on the board with a countdown focuses a teenage class far better than "when you finish".
**Do not correct in front of the class during speaking.** Note it, and deal with it at the end without naming anyone. At this age, public correction stops the speaking for a week, not a lesson.

blocks.heading: Openers: five minutes, no preparation
text: For the start of a lesson, especially a lesson after lunch or last thing in the afternoon.

blocks.name: Would you rather
blocks.language: Giving opinions and reasons; *I'd rather ... because ...*
steps: Write one choice on the board: *Would you rather be able to fly or to be invisible?*
Pairs choose and give one reason each. Thirty seconds, no more.
Take a show of hands, then hear two reasons from each side.
Learners write the next choice for the class.
blocks.variation: Keep a class list of the questions they invent, and use one at the start of every lesson.
blocks.bigClass: The hands do the counting for you. Hear four learners, not forty.

blocks.name: Three emojis
blocks.language: Past simple; describing feelings and events
steps: Draw three emojis on the board that describe your weekend, and let the class guess the story.
Learners draw three for their own weekend.
In pairs, they swap papers and guess; then the owner tells the real story in three sentences.
blocks.variation: Three emojis for a film, a match or a holiday instead.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed. Ask two pairs to share the funniest guess.

blocks.name: The lie detector
blocks.language: Question forms; past simple; short answers
steps: One learner in each group says something they did last year. It may be true or false.
The group has one minute to ask questions and decide.
The speaker admits the truth. A group that guesses right wins a point.
Rotate until everyone has spoken once.
blocks.variation: Give the sentence stems for weaker classes: *Last year I went to ..., I met ..., I tried ...*
blocks.bigClass: All groups play at the same time; keep the scores in the groups, not on the board.

blocks.name: Two-minute expert
blocks.language: Explaining; present simple; sequencing words
steps: Each learner chooses something they can genuinely do: a game, a recipe, a skill on a phone.
They explain it to their partner in one minute, and the partner must then explain it back in thirty seconds.
Swap roles.
blocks.variation: The listener has to spot one step that was missed - it turns listening into a task.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Rank these five
blocks.language: Comparatives and superlatives; agreeing and disagreeing
steps: Write five things on the board: five ways to travel, five school subjects, five jobs.
Groups must agree an order from best to worst in three minutes. Agreement is the task, not the order.
Two groups read their order and defend the top one.
blocks.variation: Hand the choosing over: each group writes the five items for another group to rank.
blocks.bigClass: Every group works at once; hear two.

blocks.heading: Games with a language point
text: Competitive, fast, and pointed at one piece of language rather than at general fun.

blocks.name: Back to the board
blocks.language: Defining and describing; *It's a thing that ...*
steps: One learner from each team sits with their back to the board.
Write a word. Their team describes it without saying the word or any part of it.
The first of the two to say the word wins the point. Change the sitter every round.
Board the phrases they need first: *It's a place where ... You use it to ...*
blocks.variation: Use only words from the last two units, and the game becomes revision.
blocks.bigClass: Four teams, four sitters, one word: the first to say it wins. It works with any class size.

blocks.name: Just a minute
blocks.language: Fluency; any known vocabulary; hesitation devices
steps: A learner speaks on an easy topic for sixty seconds without long pauses.
The group counts the pauses rather than interrupting.
Teach two fillers first - *Well, let me think, the thing is* - and they will notice the difference immediately.
Everyone takes a turn; the group's best time goes on the board.
blocks.variation: Thirty seconds for A2 classes; ninety for confident B1.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of four run at once, so twenty-four learners each speak in ten minutes.

blocks.name: Find the connection
blocks.language: Explaining and reasoning; *because*, *which means*, *they are both ...*
steps: Write three unconnected words on the board: *a train, a wedding, rice.*
Groups have three minutes to argue a connection between all three. Any connection is allowed if they can defend it.
Each group gives its connection in one sentence; the class judges which is the most convincing, not the most likely.
Play a second round with words the groups write for each other.
blocks.variation: Two words for a weaker class; four for a strong one.
blocks.bigClass: Groups work at the same time; hear four and let the class vote by hands.

blocks.name: Taboo topics
blocks.prep: None, or word cards if you have them
blocks.language: Circumlocution: saying something when you do not know the word
steps: Learner A must describe a word without using it or three other obvious words you name.
B guesses. Swap after each word.
Point out that this is the most useful real-life skill in the lesson: explaining around a word you have forgotten.
blocks.variation: Learners write the cards for the other half of the class.
blocks.bigClass: Every pair plays at once from the same list on the board.

blocks.name: Story dice, without dice
blocks.language: Past tenses; sequencing; invention
steps: Each learner writes one noun on a slip and puts it face down in the middle.
The group turns them over and must build one story that uses all four words.
Three minutes to agree the story, then one learner tells it to another group.
The best story goes to the class.
blocks.variation: Add a rule: the story must end with a question for the listeners.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed - the groups never need to hear each other.

blocks.heading: Opinions and discussion
text: For classes that can hold a short conversation, on subjects teenagers actually argue about.

blocks.name: Four corners
blocks.prep: Four signs, or four named corners
blocks.language: Agreeing and disagreeing; giving reasons
steps: Name the corners: strongly agree, agree, disagree, strongly disagree.
Read a statement: *Phones should be allowed in class.* Learners stand in the corner that fits them.
Each corner agrees one reason and says it. Anyone may change corner afterwards, and should say why.
Three statements are enough.
blocks.variation: Learners write the statements. They are better at it than we are.
blocks.bigClass: Rows instead of corners: stand up, sit down, or raise one hand for each level of agreement.

blocks.name: The interview chair
blocks.language: Question forms; present and past simple
steps: One learner sits at the front as a character of their choice - a famous person, a character from a film, an older version of themselves.
The class asks questions in role; the learner answers as the character.
After one round, everyone does it in pairs so that everybody speaks.
Give three question stems on the board for anyone stuck.
blocks.variation: Nobody sits at the front: pairs interview each other from the start, and two volunteer to repeat theirs for the class.
blocks.bigClass: Do the pair version; it needs no space and everyone speaks.

blocks.name: Change one rule
blocks.language: *Should*; *would*; reasons and consequences
steps: Each group may change one school rule. They must agree which, and give three reasons.
Each group presents in one minute; the class asks one hard question.
Vote for the most convincing change.
blocks.variation: Change a rule at home, in the town, or in a sport instead.
blocks.bigClass: Only four groups present; the rest hand in their three reasons in writing.

blocks.name: Balloon debate
blocks.language: Persuading; comparatives; *because, so, that's why*
steps: Each learner in a group takes the role of a person or a job: a doctor, a farmer, a teacher, a footballer, an engineer.
The balloon is falling; one must go. Each speaks for thirty seconds on why they should stay.
The group votes - not for themselves - and one is out. Repeat until two remain.
The survivors from each group face the class.
blocks.variation: Objects instead of people: which five things would you keep if you had to give up the rest?
blocks.bigClass: Groups of five run simultaneously; one finalist from each of four groups takes the class round.

blocks.name: Agree or disagree lines
blocks.language: Opinions; *I think ... What about you?*
steps: Two lines face each other. One line argues for, the other against, whatever they privately think.
Say a statement; pairs argue for forty seconds.
One line moves one place; new partner, new statement.
After three rounds, lines swap sides and argue the opposite.
blocks.variation: The last round is free: argue what you actually believe.
blocks.bigClass: Make four short lines rather than two long ones.

blocks.heading: Longer tasks: one lesson or two
text: When speaking needs a purpose beyond practice, and a product at the end.

blocks.name: Pitch it
blocks.language: Presenting; persuading; *it helps you to ...*
steps: Each group invents a product that solves a problem teenagers actually have.
They prepare a sixty-second pitch: what it is, who it is for, why it is better.
Groups pitch; the class scores each on usefulness and clarity, not on English.
The winning pitch is repeated to another class if you can arrange it.
blocks.variation: Pitch an app, a club, a school trip or a charity event instead.
blocks.bigClass: Groups pitch to two other groups rather than to the whole class; only the best two reach the front.

blocks.name: The news team
blocks.language: Past simple and present perfect; reporting
steps: Each group is a news team covering something that happened in the school or town this month.
Roles: presenter, reporter, two people interviewed.
They prepare a two-minute bulletin with at least two interview questions.
Perform to the class or record on a phone.
blocks.variation: Invent the news: a story from the year 2050.
blocks.bigClass: Half the groups perform this lesson, half the next.

blocks.name: Design the perfect school day
blocks.language: Times; *we would start at ...*; giving reasons
steps: Groups design a school day from start to finish, with times, and must justify three decisions.
They write the timetable on a sheet and display it.
The class walks round, reads them, and asks one question of each group.
Vote for the day most learners would choose.
blocks.variation: Design a school week, or a perfect classroom instead.
blocks.bigClass: Displaying on the wall means nobody has to present from the front.

blocks.name: The advice column
blocks.language: *Should*; suggestions; sympathising
steps: Pairs write a short problem for a teenage advice page - a safe, everyday one: too much homework, a lost phone, an argument with a friend.
Problems are swapped with another pair, who prepare spoken advice with three suggestions.
The two pairs meet: one reads the problem aloud, the other gives the advice.
The class hears the two best.
blocks.variation: You supply the problems if the class would rather not write their own.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs work simultaneously; problems are swapped within a row.

blocks.name: Teach the class something
blocks.prep: Learners may bring one object or picture
blocks.language: Explaining; imperatives; sequencing
steps: Each learner prepares a two-minute lesson on something they know that others do not.
Give the language of instruction: *First, take ... Next, you need to ... Be careful not to ...*
In groups of four, each teaches their two minutes; the group must ask two questions.
Two volunteers teach the whole class.
blocks.variation: Everyone teaches something from the same field - a sport, a dish, a phone trick - so the language repeats.
blocks.bigClass: Groups of four means every learner teaches within ten minutes, whatever the class size.

items.title: My teenagers just will not speak. Where do I start?
text: Pairs, a role, and a visible time limit. Start with Three emojis or Would you rather, where the answer cannot be wrong and the audience is one person. Whole-class speaking is the last step, not the first.

items.title: They speak, but in their own language.
text: Give a short window - "English only for three minutes" - and put the exact phrases they need on the board first. Most first-language use at this age is a missing phrase, not defiance. Team points for English-only minutes work better than telling off.

items.title: A few loud learners dominate every activity.
text: Use activities with a fixed turn: Just a minute, the balloon debate, the lie detector. When everybody has a numbered turn, the quiet ones speak and the loud ones wait, without you having to say so.

items.title: Are games not a waste of a lesson?
text: A game with a language point is practice with attention on the meaning, which is when language sticks. Back to the board drills defining language harder than any exercise. A game without a language point is the waste.

items.title: How do I mark or assess speaking activities?
text: Do not mark most of them. Choose one activity a month, listen to four or five learners against three criteria you have shown the class beforehand, and keep a note. Trying to assess everyone every time is why speaking gets dropped.

pages.title: How to Make an ESL Lesson Plan
pages.metaTitle: How to Make an ESL Lesson Plan: A Practical Guide
pages.description: How to make an ESL lesson plan: aims as learner outcomes, a staged procedure with timings, and a blank plan to copy. A practical guide for teachers.
pages.keywords: how to make an ESL lesson plan, ESL lesson planning, lesson plan template ESL, how to plan an English lesson, aims for ESL lessons
pages.teaches: Lesson planning for English language teachers

hero.text: A lesson plan is not a form to fill in for an inspector. It is the set of decisions you make before the lesson so that you do not have to make them in front of thirty people.

blocks.heading: Why bother
text: This guide takes you through those decisions in the order they are actually made, with the wording to use, the two mistakes that cause most weak lessons, and a blank plan you can copy.

blocks.heading: 1. Start at the end: what will they be able to do?
text: Write the aim as something learners will be able to *do*, not as something you will cover. "Present perfect" is a topic, not an aim. "Learners will be able to ask about and describe life experiences with *Have you ever ...?*" is an aim, because you can see whether it happened.
The test is simple: at the end of the lesson, could you point at a learner and say whether they can do it? If not, the aim is too vague to plan from.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Write the aim first and the activities second. Most weak lessons are a list of activities with an aim added afterwards.

blocks.heading: 2. Decide what the language actually is
text: Take the language you are teaching and look at three things before the lesson, not during it: what it **means**, how it is **formed**, and how it **sounds**.

Write two or three questions that check the meaning without using the grammar name. For the past simple: *Is it finished? Do we know when?* These are concept-checking questions, and they save you from the answer every teacher has heard - *yes, teacher* - when you ask "do you understand?"
Then write down what your learners will get wrong, and what you will do about each one. A problem you have predicted takes a minute to fix; one that surprises you takes ten.

blocks.title: In practice
text: If you cannot say what the language means in one plain sentence, you are not ready to teach it yet.

blocks.heading: 3. Choose a shape for the lesson
text: **PPP** - presentation, practice, production - suits a new, small piece of language: you show it, they practise it, they use it. It is the easiest shape to control with a large class.
**Test-teach-test** suits language learners have met before: let them try it first, see what is broken, teach that, then let them try again. Better than PPP when the class half-knows something.
**Task-based** suits a class that needs to do something real - make a plan, solve a problem - with the language taught where it is needed. It gives the most speaking and needs the most confidence.
Whichever you choose, controlled practice comes before free practice. Learners cannot be accurate and creative at the same time.

blocks.title: In practice
text: One shape per lesson. Mixing two is how a lesson loses its direction halfway through.

blocks.heading: 4. Give every stage a time and an interaction pattern
text: Beside each stage write the minutes and who talks to whom: whole class, individual, pairs, groups, mingle. Two lines in a plan, and they prevent the lesson where the teacher talks for forty minutes.
Add up the times. If the total is longer than the lesson - and it will be, the first few times - cut a stage rather than hurry all of them.
Aim to have learners speaking to each other for at least half the lesson. In a class of forty, that is the only way most of them speak at all.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Plan the change of pattern, not just the activity: "in pairs" written down is a decision; decided in the moment, it becomes "work with your friend" and chaos.

blocks.heading: 5. Write the instructions you will say
text: Write the three or four sentences you will actually use to set each task, in the shortest words you can. Long instructions are the commonest cause of a class not doing what you asked.
Then write one instruction-checking question for any task that could be misunderstood: *Do you write or speak? Do you work alone or with a partner? How long have you got?*
Plan to demonstrate rather than explain wherever you can. Doing one round with a strong learner is worth three sentences of description.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Give the instruction, then hand out the paper. Do it the other way round and nobody hears the instruction.

blocks.heading: 6. Plan how you will know it worked
text: Decide before the lesson how you will check the aim: an exit task of two or three sentences, a question round the room, or a task you collect. Without this, "they seemed to understand" is all you will have.
Keep it small. Three sentences written in the last four minutes tell you more than a page of homework marked a week later.
Plan the feedback too: note mistakes while they speak, put four sentences on the board at the end - two right, two wrong - and let the class repair them. Nobody is named, and everybody learns.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Whatever your exit task is, it should be in the form the aim describes. If the aim was questions, the exit task asks for questions.

blocks.heading: 7. Plan for the class you actually have
text: **Too many learners:** turn any mingle into rows - ask the four people nearest you - and collect written work from one row each lesson rather than all of them.
**No photocopier:** put the text on the board before the lesson, or use dictation; learners write in their notebooks. Almost no good activity truly needs paper.

**Mixed levels:** plan one support - a list of the verbs, a sentence frame - and one stretch - an extra question, a harder round. Two lines in the plan, and both ends of the class have something to do.
**The lesson runs short:** keep one five-minute speaking activity in your pocket that needs no materials. The end of a lesson is not the time to invent one.

blocks.title: In practice
text: A plan that ignores your real class is a plan you will abandon in week two.

blocks.heading: A blank plan to copy
intro: Everything below fits on one side of paper. A plan you cannot see at a glance is a plan you will not look at while teaching.
rows: Class and date
Who, when, how long
Level
CEFR level, or the course level
Main aim
By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to ...
Subsidiary aims
One or two, in the same form
Target language
The sentences themselves, not the grammar name
Meaning, form, pronunciation
Concept questions; the patterns; the sounds
Anticipated problems
What they will get wrong, and your solution for each
Materials
Everything you must bring or prepare
Stages

Support and stretch
One line each
Checking learning
The exit task
Homework
If any

blocks.heading: Five mistakes that weaken a lesson
columns: What it looks like, and the fix
rows: Planning activities instead of an aim
The lesson is busy and pleasant, and at the end nobody can do anything they could not do before. Fix it by writing the aim first, and asking of every activity: does this serve it?
Too much teacher talk
The plan has no interaction patterns, so everything defaults to teacher-to-class. Write the pattern beside every stage and count the minutes learners speak.
Free practice too early
Learners are asked to use language they have not yet used accurately even once, so they avoid it. Put a controlled stage in between.
Instructions invented on the spot
The class does the wrong thing, and five minutes disappear. Write the words, demonstrate, and check with one question.
No way of knowing whether it worked
Plan the exit task when you plan the aim, not when the bell is about to go.

items.title: How long should a lesson plan be?
text: One page. A plan you cannot see at a glance is a plan you will not look at while teaching. Everything on the blank plan above fits on a single side.

items.title: Do experienced teachers still write plans?
text: They write shorter ones. The thinking does not go away - the aim, the problems, the timings - but it takes ten minutes instead of an hour, and much of it stays in the head. New teachers should write it all down, because that is how it gets into the head.

items.title: What if the lesson does not go to plan?
text: That is normal and not a failure. Keep the aim and drop a stage; the plan exists so that you know which stage can go. Note afterwards what happened, in one line, and your next plan will be better.

items.title: Should the plan be in English or my own language?
text: Whichever you think in. The plan is for you. Only the target language and the instructions you will say need to be in English, and those should be written exactly.

pages.title: How to Teach Reported Speech
pages.metaTitle: How to Teach Reported Speech: A Practical Guide
pages.description: How to teach reported speech at B1 and B2: start from a real message, teach said and told first, and treat backshift as a choice, not a law.
pages.keywords: how to teach reported speech, teaching reported speech, reported speech lesson, backshift, indirect speech teaching tips, reported questions
pages.teaches: Teaching reported speech to English language learners

hero.text: Reported speech is taught badly more often than almost any other structure, and the reason is that it is usually taught as a shifting exercise: move the tense back one, change *here* to *there*, change *yesterday* to *the day before*. Learners pass the exercise and then never use the structure to report anything.

blocks.heading: Why bother
text: This guide is about teaching it as what it is - what you say when you tell somebody what somebody else said - and about the two decisions that make the difference: when to backshift, and what to do with reported questions.

blocks.heading: 1. Start from a real report, not from a rule
text: Before any table of shifts, create something worth reporting. Tell two learners a short piece of news quietly, or send them out and back with a message. Then ask the class: *what did she say?*

Take the answers as they come, including the wrong ones, and write three or four on the board. You now have the target structure on the board in the learners' own words, and the lesson is about repairing it rather than introducing it.
This also shows them the point of the structure within the first three minutes, which a tense table never does.

blocks.title: In practice
text: If you begin with the rule, learners learn a transformation. If you begin with a message, they learn a way of speaking.

blocks.heading: 2. Teach the reporting verb before the tense shift
text: *Said, told, asked, explained, complained, admitted, promised, suggested.* The choice of verb carries most of the meaning in a real report, and it is where learners sound most obviously like a textbook.

Teach the two patterns that trip everybody up, side by side: *he told me that ...* takes a person, *he said that ...* does not. **He said me** is the single commonest error in this area at B1 and it is worth one minute of explicit attention.
Then add one verb with a different pattern - *he suggested going*, *he promised to come* - so learners see early that reporting verbs are not interchangeable.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Put *said* and *told me* at the two ends of the board and add sentences under each. Learners see the pattern before they hear the rule.

blocks.heading: 3. Teach backshift as a choice, not a law
text: The rule learners are usually given - move the tense back one - is not what speakers do. We backshift when the reporting verb is in the past **and** the thing said is finished, or over, or no longer true.

When it is still true, fluent speakers very often do not shift: *She said she lives in Kandy* is normal English, and so is *He told me he's coming tonight*. Teach both, and teach the question that decides it: **is it still true now?**

Say plainly that examinations usually expect the shift. Learners can do both: shift when a paper asks, choose when they speak. Hiding the real usage from them produces learners who correct native speakers.

blocks.title: In practice
text: One question decides most cases: *is it still true?* If yes, shifting is optional. If no, shift.

blocks.heading: 4. Do time and place words only when they are needed
text: *Yesterday - the day before, here - there, this - that, tomorrow - the next day.* These change for one reason only: because the report is being made in another place or at another time, so the original word would now point at the wrong thing.

Demonstrate it instead of listing it. Say something with *here* and *today*, then report it in the corridor the next day, and ask what has to change and why. Learners who see the reason remember it; learners given the list remember about half of it.
If you report a message in the same room a minute later, nothing changes. Show that too - it stops learners changing words that need no changing, which is a real examination error.

blocks.title: In practice
text: A word only changes when it would now point to the wrong time or the wrong place. That is the whole rule.

blocks.heading: 5. Teach reported questions separately, and expect trouble
text: Reported questions are a different structure and deserve their own stage, or their own lesson. Two changes happen at once: the word order returns to subject-verb, and the auxiliary *do* disappears. *Where do you live?* becomes *He asked me where I lived.*

The commonest error is keeping the question order: **He asked me where did I live.** Drill it in the direction learners will need it - give a question aloud, they report it - rather than only on paper.
Then add yes or no questions with *if* or *whether*: *Are you coming? - She asked if I was coming.* Learners who have met only *wh-* questions produce nothing when the question has no question word.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Write one wrong sentence on the board - *He asked me where did I live* - and let the class repair it. They remember their own repair.

blocks.heading: 6. Finish with a task that needs reporting to work
text: Practice is not a gap-fill. Use a task where reporting is the only way to get the information across: a rumour passed along a line, an interview reported to a third person, a message taken for somebody who was absent, or a discussion summarised by a note-taker.
Give the reporting verbs on the board and require three different ones. Without that, everything comes back as *said*, and the vocabulary half of the lesson disappears.

Collect four sentences from what you hear, two correct and two not, and put them on the board unnamed at the end. The class repairs them. That is the correction stage, and it is where the *said me* and the *where did I live* finally go.

blocks.title: In practice
text: If learners could do the task without reporting anybody's words, it is not practice for this lesson.

blocks.heading: A sixty-minute shape for a reported speech lesson
intro: One way to put the six steps above into a single lesson. The lesson plan on this site follows this shape, with the stages timed.
rows: Lead-in (5 min)
A message carried and delivered. *What did she say?* Answers go on the board as they come.
Clarify meaning (8 min)
Why we report: we were not there, or we are telling somebody else. Concept questions on one sentence.
Reporting verbs (7 min)
*Said* and *told me* contrasted. One verb with a different pattern added.
Backshift (12 min)
Guided discovery from the board sentences. The *is it still true?* question. Examination expectations stated.
Controlled practice (10 min)
Spoken transformation first, then five written sentences. Check in pairs before the class.
Reported questions (8 min)
Word order and the disappearing *do*. One wrong sentence repaired by the class.
Freer practice (8 min)
A task where reporting is the only way to pass the information on. Three different reporting verbs required.
Feedback (2 min)
Four sentences on the board, two right and two wrong, nobody named.

blocks.heading: Six mistakes that make the lesson fail
columns: What it looks like, and the fix
rows: Starting with the tense table
Learners learn to shift tenses and still cannot report what a friend told them. Begin with a message somebody has to pass on, and get the structure onto the board from the learners.
Teaching backshift as compulsory

Learners then produce *She said she lived in Kandy* about somebody who still lives there, and hear natural English as wrong. Teach the *is it still true?* question and say openly what examinations expect.
Ignoring said and told
*He said me* survives for years because nobody spent a minute on it. Contrast the two patterns explicitly, early, with examples under each.
Only teaching said
Reports in real life use *told, asked, explained, complained, admitted, promised*. Put four on the board and require three of them in the final task.
Putting reported questions in the same stage
Two changes at once - word order and the lost auxiliary - is too much beside backshift. Give questions their own stage or their own lesson.
Practising only in writing
The error learners need to lose is one of word order under time pressure, which only appears when they speak. Do the spoken transformation before the written one.

items.title: Is backshift really optional?
text: When the reporting verb is past and the reported information is still true, yes: *She said she lives in Kandy* and *She said she lived in Kandy* are both correct, and the first is very common in speech. When the information is finished or no longer true, the shift is normal. Examinations usually want the shift, so teach both and say which is which.

items.title: Which tenses do not shift back?
text: Past perfect has nowhere further to go, so it stays. Modals *would, could, might, should* and *ought to* stay. *Must* usually becomes *had to* when it means obligation. And nothing shifts after a present reporting verb: *he says he is tired*.

items.title: Should I teach the whole tense table at once?
text: No. Take present simple and present continuous into the past in the first lesson, add past simple and *will* in the second, and leave modals until learners are reporting confidently. A complete table on day one is copied, not learnt.

items.title: How do I teach it in a class of forty?
text: Everything here works in pairs. The lead-in message needs two learners; the transformation drill is teacher to whole class; the final task is pairs or groups of three reporting to each other. Nobody has to come to the front.

items.title: What about reported orders and requests?
text: They belong in a later lesson: *He told me to wait*, *She asked me not to be late* - verb plus object plus infinitive, and no *that*. Adding them to a lesson that already covers statements, questions and backshift guarantees that something is lost.

items.title: Is there a ready-made lesson for this?
text: Yes. The reported speech lesson plan on this site follows the shape above, with timings, concept-checking questions, anticipated problems and a printable worksheet with answers.

pages.description: How to teach English speaking in an ordinary class: more talking time, the language on the board, thinking time, and what to do about correction.

pages.teaches: Teaching speaking to English language learners

hero.text: Most learners who have studied English for years still cannot speak it. That is not usually because they lack vocabulary or grammar: it is because they have spent those years not speaking.

blocks.heading: Why bother
text: This guide is about how to change that in an ordinary class - forty learners, forty minutes, no equipment - and what to do about the three problems every teacher meets: silence, the first language, and correction.

blocks.heading: 1. Count the minutes learners actually speak
text: Before changing anything, measure it. In your next lesson, note roughly how many minutes learners speak English to each other. In most classrooms, in most countries, the honest answer is under five out of forty.

The number matters more than any method. A class of forty where everyone talks in pairs for ten minutes produces four hundred learner-minutes of speaking. The same class answering the teacher one at a time produces forty at best, and one learner speaks while thirty-nine wait.
Fix a target - half the lesson, in pairs or groups - and plan backwards from it.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Whole-class question and answer feels like speaking practice to the teacher and looks like listening practice to the learners.

blocks.heading: 2. Give the language before the task
text: A learner cannot invent *Have you ever ...?* while also thinking what to say. Put the two or three structures the task needs on the board, drill them once chorally, and leave them there.

Add the small phrases that keep a conversation alive, which coursebooks often skip: *Really? Why do you think so? What about you? I'm not sure.* These are what make an exchange last more than two turns.
For weaker classes, give a sentence frame with a gap. *My favourite ... is ... because ...* is not childish; it is the scaffolding that gets a first sentence out.

blocks.title: In practice
text: If nobody is speaking, the usual cause is not shyness but a missing phrase. Check the board before you blame the class.

blocks.heading: 3. Plan the thinking time
text: Thirty seconds of silence before speaking doubles what most learners say, and it is the cheapest improvement available.
Let them make notes - words, not sentences. Notes in full sentences turn a speaking activity into reading aloud, so give a limit: three words, or five.

For anything harder than personal facts, let them try it once in pairs before any of it is said in front of the class. The second telling is always better, which is why rehearsal, not performance, is where the learning happens.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Rehearse, then report. Never ask a learner to speak in front of the class about something they have not already said once to one person.

blocks.heading: 4. Build tasks with a reason to speak
text: The strongest speaking tasks have an information gap: one person knows something the other needs. Spot-the-difference, find someone who, interviewing and reporting back, describing a route - all of these make speaking necessary rather than decorative.
The weakest task is "discuss this in pairs" with nothing to produce. Give an outcome: agree an order, find three differences, choose one plan, report your partner's answer.
Set a visible time limit and stop the task while learners still have something to say. A task that runs until it dies teaches learners that speaking is dull.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Ask of any speaking task: why would anyone say this to another human being? If there is no answer, the task needs an outcome.

blocks.heading: 5. Handle the first language sensibly
text: Some first-language use is normal and useful, especially in the planning stage. What matters is the speaking stage itself.
Set a short window rather than a permanent ban: "English only for these three minutes" is enforceable, and "never use your own language" is not.
Where a class slips into the first language constantly, look at the task before the discipline: it is usually too hard, too vague, or missing the language it needs.

blocks.title: In practice
text: A monitor in each group - one learner whose job for that task is to keep the group in English - works far better than the teacher policing the room.

blocks.heading: 6. Correct later, not during
text: While learners speak, do not interrupt. Walk round with a pen and write down what you hear: two or three errors that several learners made, and two or three good sentences.
At the end, put four sentences on the board - two correct, two with the errors - and let the class find and repair them. Nobody is named, and the good sentences get read out with credit.
Correct on the spot only when the error blocks understanding, or when it is the exact language you have just taught.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Public correction during speaking costs you more speaking in every later lesson than the error ever cost.

blocks.heading: 7. Make it work in a class of forty
text: **Pairs, always.** Everyone speaks at once; you do not need to hear it all. Forty learners in pairs is twenty conversations, which is exactly the point.
**Rows instead of mingles.** Where learners cannot move, they ask the four people nearest them, then everyone moves one seat along once.
**Sample, do not assess everyone.** Listen properly to four or five learners each lesson and keep a note. In eight lessons you have heard everybody, and nobody waited.
**Use the room's own noise as a measure.** A speaking task should sound loud. Silence in a speaking activity means the task has failed, not that the class is well behaved.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Large classes are better for speaking practice than small ones, because there are more partners. What they are worse for is the teacher hearing it all - so stop trying to.

blocks.heading: 8. Assess speaking without dread
text: Tell learners the three things you will listen for before they speak - for example: the target language used, ideas connected with *and, but, because*, and being understood without repeating.
Assess a few learners at a time, during ordinary tasks, over several lessons. A separate speaking examination for a class of forty costs a week of lessons and tells you little more.
Give each learner one thing done well and one thing to change. A list of six weaknesses changes nothing.

blocks.title: In practice
text: Learners who know the criteria before they speak perform better against them. Secret criteria measure guessing.

blocks.heading: A blank plan to copy
intro: Everything below fits on one side of paper. A plan you cannot see at a glance is a plan you will not look at while teaching.
rows: Before the task
The language on the board, drilled once
Thinking time
30 seconds, notes in words only
Rehearsal
In pairs, everyone at once
The task
An outcome to produce, and a visible time limit
Change partner
Repeat once - the second telling is the fluent one

Two or three learners only, on what a partner said
Feedback

Your note
Four or five learners heard properly, written down

blocks.heading: Five mistakes that weaken a lesson
columns: What it looks like, and the fix
rows: Asking the class a question and waiting
One learner answers and thirty-nine listen. Put every question into pairs first, then hear two answers.
No language on the board
Learners want to speak and cannot find the words, so they stop or switch language. Two structures and three short phrases fix most of it.
No outcome
"Discuss in pairs" produces thirty seconds of talk. Give something to agree, find, choose or report.
Correcting while they speak
The speaking stops, and next time it starts later. Collect errors and deal with them at the end, unnamed.
Letting the task run too long
Stop while they still have something to say. Two short tasks beat one long one.

items.title: My learners understand English but will not speak. What do I do first?
text: Pairs, a sentence frame on the board, thirty seconds of thinking time, and a task with an outcome. Start with facts they cannot get wrong - their own routine, their own weekend - before anything that needs an opinion.

items.title: Is it worth doing speaking work if the examination is written?
text: Yes, and it improves the writing. Learners who have said an idea aloud write it faster and more accurately. Speaking is also the fastest way to find out what the class has actually understood.

items.title: How can I hear forty learners?
text: You cannot, and you do not need to. Listen properly to four or five each lesson, note what you hear, and rotate. Over a month you will have heard everyone, and the class will have spoken in every lesson.

items.title: What about pronunciation?
text: Teach it inside the speaking task, not as a separate subject: the sounds of the target language, the stress in the phrases on the board, and the linking between words. Two minutes of drilling before a task is worth more than a whole lesson on the phonemic chart.

items.title: Do online classes change any of this?
text: The principles stay; the mechanics change. Breakout rooms replace pairs, and the teacher hears less, so give clearer outcomes and ask for something written in the chat at the end so you know what happened.
